topicName: EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) - Instance Types, AMIs, Security Groups, Key Pairs
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) - Instance Types, AMIs, Security Groups, Key Pairs"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) is a web service that provides resizable compute capacity in the cloud. It allows you to rent virtual servers (EC2 instances) for running your applications. This tutorial covers key EC2 concepts: Instance Types, Amazon Machine Images (AMIs), Security Groups, and Key Pairs."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Instance Types"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"EC2 Instance Types provide different combinations of CPU, memory, storage, and networking capacity. Choose an instance type based on the resource requirements of your application. Instance types are categorized into families, such as general purpose, compute optimized, memory optimized, accelerated computing, and storage optimized."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"General Purpose (e.g., t3.micro, m5.large): Balanced compute, memory, and networking resources. Suitable for web servers, small databases, and development environments."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Compute Optimized (e.g., c5.large): High-performance processors. Ideal for compute-intensive applications like batch processing, media transcoding, and high-performance web servers."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Memory Optimized (e.g., r5.large): Large memory footprint. Suitable for memory-intensive applications like in-memory databases (e.g., Redis, Memcached) and big data processing."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Accelerated Computing (e.g., p3.2xlarge, g4dn.xlarge): Use hardware accelerators, or co-processors, to perform some functions more efficiently than is possible in software running on a CPU. Examples include graphics processing (GPUs) and field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). Ideal for machine learning, video encoding, and scientific simulations."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Storage Optimized (e.g., i3.large): High disk I/O performance. Suitable for NoSQL databases (e.g., Cassandra, MongoDB), data warehousing, and log processing."},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"When selecting an instance type, consider factors like vCPUs, memory (RAM), storage (instance store or EBS), network performance, and cost."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Amazon Machine Images (AMIs)"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"An Amazon Machine Image (AMI) is a template that contains the software configuration (operating system, application server, and applications) required to launch your instance. You can choose from a variety of public AMIs provided by AWS, AWS Marketplace, or create your own custom AMIs."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Public AMIs: Provided by AWS and the AWS community. They are pre-configured with common operating systems like Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, Windows Server, and others."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"AWS Marketplace AMIs: Offered by third-party vendors. They often include pre-installed software and tools, such as databases, security appliances, and development tools."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Custom AMIs: Created by you. You can customize an existing AMI by installing software, configuring settings, and then creating a new AMI from the instance. This allows you to quickly launch instances with your desired configuration."},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"When choosing an AMI, consider the operating system, pre-installed software, region, and architecture (e.g., 64-bit x86, ARM)."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Security Groups"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Security Group acts as a virtual firewall for your EC2 instances. It controls inbound and outbound traffic at the instance level. You define rules that specify which traffic is allowed to reach your instance and which traffic is allowed to leave your instance."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Inbound Rules: Control the traffic that can reach your instance (e.g., allowing SSH access on port 22, HTTP access on port 80, HTTPS access on port 443)."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Outbound Rules: Control the traffic that can leave your instance (e.g., allowing access to the internet on ports 80 and 443)."},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"Security Groups are stateful, meaning that if you allow inbound traffic on a specific port, the response traffic is automatically allowed to leave the instance, regardless of the outbound rules. You can associate multiple security groups with an instance."},{"order":22,"type":"code","text":"Example Security Group Rule (Allow SSH access from your IP):
Type: SSH
Protocol: TCP
Port Range: 22
Source: Your IP Address (e.g., 203.0.113.0/24)"},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Pairs"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Key Pair consists of a public key and a private key. AWS stores the public key, and you store the private key. When you launch an EC2 instance, you specify a key pair. You use the private key to securely connect to your instance."},{"order":25,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Key pairs are used for SSH access to Linux instances and for decrypting the administrator password for Windows instances."},{"order":26,"type":"bullet_point","text":"It is crucial to keep your private key secure. If you lose your private key, you will not be able to connect to your instance (unless you have configured alternative access methods)."},{"order":27,"type":"code","text":"Example SSH command to connect to an EC2 instance:
ssh -i 'your-private-key.pem' ec2-user@<public-ip-address>"},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"Best Practice: Use different key pairs for different environments (e.g., development, staging, production) to improve security."},{"order":29,"type":"paragraph","text":"By understanding Instance Types, AMIs, Security Groups, and Key Pairs, you can effectively launch and manage EC2 instances to meet your application's needs."}]
